extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, critics, and playwrights studying Aristotle's Poetics and dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Aristotelian criteria for writing and evaluating tragic drama, focusing on plot (μῦθος), character (ἦθος), and thought (διάνοια), and the qualities of the ideal tragic hero. Useful for literary analysis and dramatic writing grounded in classical theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (μῦθος) as first principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Or the six elements into which Aristotle analyses a tragedy, plot (μῦθος) holds the first place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot is the artistic equivalent of 'action' in real life: the imitation of an action and of life (μίμησις πράξεως καὶ βίου). It embraces deeds, incidents, situations, mental processes and motives which work together towards a definite end. The plot is the 'soul' or animating principle of tragedy and is the primary principle on which the play's meaning and emotional effect depend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy must excite pity and fear (emotional aim)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal tragedy will 'excite pity and fear in no ordinary combination' and heighten these emotions to their utmost capacity under perfect art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The arrangement of incidents in the plot (including reversals and recognitions) should be organized to produce the distinctive tragic feeling appropriate to tragedy. The plot's structure should realize the play's intention (τέλος) and through it the intended emotional response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex plot preferred (πεπλεγμένη)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal tragedy is of the type technically known in the Poetics as 'complex' (πεπλεγμένη), not simple (ἀπλῆ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complex plot combines the Change of Fortune (μετάβασις) with Reversal of the Situation (περιπέτεια) or with Recognition (ἀναγνώρισις), or with both. Such elements intensify dramatic effect and are characteristic of the 'ideal tragedy' described by Aristotle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (περιπέτεια / reversal) must be effective
rubrics_metrics.description: Περιπέτεια denotes a striking change in the course of a scene or a series of incidents that turn upon the agent and catch him in the recoil; it may involve an intention being overruled to produce an opposite effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peripeteia can manifest as reversal of intention or as a change of situation within a scene; it is distinct from but related to μετάβασις (change of fortune) and sometimes approaches what modern critics call 'irony of destiny.' Use peripeteia as a device that charges deeds with fuller, often opposite, meaning and heightens tragic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action (πρᾶξις) must be inwardly motivated and outwardly manifested
rubrics_metrics.description: The πρᾶξις of the drama springs from the inward power of will and manifests itself in external doing; it includes outward fortune and misfortune as well as the mental processes which produce action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic action should not be merely external events (εὐτυχία/δυστυχία) but should represent a mode of moral energy or activity — deeds together with the motives and thoughts that generate them. The plot must therefore integrate inner motives with outward incidents to be truly dramatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ἦθος) as moral element revealed in speech and action
rubrics_metrics.description: ἦθος is the moral element in character; it reveals the state or direction of the will and is an expression of moral purpose as manifested in speeches and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic ἦθος should make the character's preairé̄sis (choice/volition) apparent; ethical disposition must be visible in what characters do and say. While character determines action, Aristotle places character subsidiary to plot — characters should be credible causes of the actions that drive the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dianoia (διάνοια) as the intellectual element in drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Διάνοια is the thought or intellectual element implied in rational conduct; it includes intellectual reflections, proofs, disproofs, and general maxims as given in dramatic λόγοι.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dianoia is typically embodied in speech (λόγοι) and is connected to rhetorical and dialectical aspects of drama (argumentation, enthymeme, maxims). It helps prepare and supply the πάθη (passions/effects) among characters and contributes to the logical and persuasive structure of scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity/probability must govern plot, speeches, and actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of necessity or probability prescribed for the plot shall apply also to the speeches and actions of the dramatic persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions, incidents and speeches must be credible within the play's logic — they should follow from character and circumstance by necessity or probability so that the evolution of the plot and the characters' responses feel organically justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting ethical monologues for plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferior writers attempted to make ethical monologues (ῥήσεις ἠθικαὶ) take the place of a well-constructed plot; such sequences do not produce a tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a succession of moral speeches or didactic dialogues as the main vehicle of a tragedy. Tragedy requires action; ethical discourse without action is at best preliminary material, not the tragic core.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character must be revealed through action not mere description
rubrics_metrics.description: In the drama the characters are not described, they enact their own story and so reveal themselves; we know them by their performance before our eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic character-drawing should show persons producing an action (characters producing action) rather than depend on external narration. While a play with a strong plot and weak delineation of character may be dramatic, ideal tragedy integrates convincing individual character-complexity with plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic hero should be neither faultlessly faultless nor consummate villain
rubrics_metrics.description: No 'faultily faultless' hero, any more than a consummate villain, can inspire so vital a sympathy as the hero whose weakness and whose strength alike bring him within the range of our common humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tragic hero should be a noble or elevated nature with a defect or frailty (ἁμαρτία/weakness) that grows and culminates in disaster; modern drama has enlarged the notion of hamartia to include the process by which a frailty expands into tragic ruin (e.g., Hamlet, Othello, Lear). The hero's mixture of admirable qualities and tragic flaw arouses pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as organic design: beginning, middle and end (τέλος)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot is the beginning and the end; it gives the play its inner meaning and reality and is the end (τέλος) of a tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the plot as an organic unity (like a living organism) where parts grow round a nucleus; the plot's design (outline) is the groundwork through which character and colour obtain meaning. Without a cohesive beginning, middle and end aimed at a telos, the tragic effect cannot be properly achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Aristotle's rules as guidance, not rigid law
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's manner is allusive and incomplete; he writes tentatively and throws out suggestions without guarding against misconception, so the Poetics should not be strained into an inflexible code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the Poetics with caution: its aphorisms and fragmentary form warn against dogmatic application. Where historical practice or dramatic aims suggest variation (as in Shakespeare), adapt rather than forcibly harmonize plays to fit a literal reading of Aristotle.
